summary: An informational memo about producing PostScript and PDF documents that print well on both North American and international paper sizes, since these formats fix page layout exactly and the common paper sizes differ.

eli5.summary: Paper in some countries is a bit different in size. This memo gives tips so a document prints nicely on either kind.

questions: a4 vs letter paper in pdf
what margins make a pdf print on a4 and letter
how to print a letter pdf on a4
subtitle: Margin advice so a PDF or PostScript file prints on both US Letter and A4 paper.

tldr.problem: PostScript and PDF fix the page layout exactly, but North America uses Letter paper and most of the rest of the world uses A4, so a document made for one may not print well on the other.
tldr.mechanism: The memo gives three methods: use wider margins when creating the file, print at reduced size, or buy A4 paper.
tldr.outcome: Following its margin advice makes documents printable on both formats; the memo also recommends PDF over PostScript for distribution.

facts.label: Letter margin rule
facts.value: Left and right at least 21 mm

facts.label: A4 margin rule
facts.value: Top and bottom at least 33 mm

today: RFC 2346 is an Informational memo from May 1998, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is practical advice, not a standard.

sections.title: The Letter versus A4 Problem
sections.content:
PostScript (application/postscript, .ps) and Portable Document Format (application/pdf, .pdf) specify exactly how a printed page looks. North America uses Letter, 216 x 279 mm (8.5 x 11 in), while the ISO-standard A4 is 210 x 297 mm (8.3 x 11.7 in).

So Letter is 6 mm wider and A4 is 18 mm taller. A document formatted on one continent may not print properly on another. The memo is not aimed at HTML, though it may help HTML developers who use fixed-size graphics and fixed WIDTH sizes.
sections.eli5: One kind of paper is a little wider and the other is a little taller. A page made to fill one can get cut off on the other.

sections.title: Method 1: Wider Margins
sections.content:
The sender leaves extra margin so the text fits on both sizes. The short version is: on Letter, keep left and right margins at least 21 mm (0.8 in); on A4, keep top and bottom margins at least 33 mm (1.3 in). The table gives the full suggested minimums for each size and orientation.

The margin is added to both top and bottom (or both sides) because the sender does not know which way the recipient's printer feeds paper. Left and right margins on any format should be at least 20 mm to suit ISO 838 filing hole punches. Headers, footers and page numbers must also be inside the margins, since many word processors place them outside.
sections.eli5: Leave a wide empty border all around. Then it does not matter which kind of paper you print on.

sections.title: Methods 2 and 3: Reduce Size or Buy A4
sections.content:
In Method 2 the sender prints at 100 percent, and the recipient prints at 94 percent of full size or less, if the printing program allows it. Many PostScript printing programs do not, so the recipient may convert to PDF first, for example with Adobe Acrobat Distiller or recent versions of ghostscript. The recipient may also need to give the paper size actually loaded in the printer.

Method 3 suggests that people in North America who often print international documents buy A4 paper, which is available from many large paper distributors and supported by almost all laser printers.

The authors recommend PDF over PostScript, citing the shrink to fit printing option, per-page compression, display before full download, portability, better font rendering and embedded URLs.
sections.eli5: You can also shrink the page a little when printing, or just buy the other size of paper.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo says following its advice makes it more likely a document reads and looks the same for all recipients, reducing the risk of misunderstanding, and that it introduces no known new security risks. It notes that writers might become too sure their documents will look identical everywhere.

It also states that PostScript has well known security risks, which are discussed in RFC 2046.
sections.eli5: Following the advice is safe. Just do not assume every printout will look exactly the same.
